title: The 2025 Allens AI Australian law benchmark
author: Allens

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal benchmarks: Realistic tasks expose uneven competence
st.an: The source accepts the need for realistic, task-specific and jurisdiction-sensitive evaluation, then materially extends the cluster through a repeatable Australian-law benchmark using expert, scaled grading to detect nuance and foreign-law intrusion. Its explicit single-prompt and task-coverage limitations reinforce the cluster’s warning that conclusions depend on prompts, scope and grading, although the supplied material provides no numerical performance results.
qs: While the relative benefits of LLM-marked and human-marked frameworks have been discussed elsewhere, a human-marking process allows our benchmark to consider and distinguish nuanced behaviours that arise with each question.
Such prompting, however, does not explore the results that can be achieved by carefully refining queries for each LLM or by interrogating and testing LLM responses in subsequent prompts.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: Allens accepts the need for realistic, reproducible legal-AI evaluation and materially extends it through jurisdiction-specific expert grading, scaled question-level assessment and explicit protocol limitations. Its findings of uneven performance reinforce that aggregate model scores do not establish consistent practical competence.
qs: Such prompting, however, does not explore the results that can be achieved by carefully refining queries for each LLM or by interrogating and testing LLM responses in subsequent prompts.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: Allens accepts the need for task-specific, expert-led evaluation and materially develops it through a repeatable Australian-law benchmark: fixed legal tasks, standardised prompting, repeated queries, specialist scoring of substance, citations and clarity, and central moderation. The source explains methodology rather than demonstrating deployment outcomes or making recommendations.
qs: The 2025 edition of this benchmark has asked the same questions as were posed in 2024, in order to deliver both an absolute assessment of LLM performance over time, and to allow for the relative assessment of different LLMs at a given moment in time.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: Allens directly supports the cluster’s proposition that high average benchmark scores establish bounded capability rather than dependable autonomous legal performance. Its results combine sharp year-on-year improvement with variable, sometimes seriously incorrect answers, weak citation reliability, jurisdictional contamination and explicit limits on reliance; it therefore recommends expert-supervised, task-specific use.
qs: - The average *substance *score of all the LLMs we tested was higher in 2025 (4.3** out of **5**) than in 2024 (**1.92** out of **5**), confirming the overall improvement across the board through the year, including with the appearance of the new generation of reasoning models (such as DeepSeek and OpenAI o1).
Disclaimer  No reliance should be placed on any LLMs or their responses, even in cases where specific answers or LLM performances have been positively marked.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: Allens accepts the cluster’s core proposition: LLMs can accelerate and assist legal work, but current systems do not provide consistently reliable legal advice, and improvements in safeguards do not displace the need for legal expertise and human judgment.
qs: As our benchmarking shows, the current generation of large language models (LLMs) still falls short of the critical analysis skills required to deliver consistently reliable legal advice.
In legal practice, LLMs are safest and most effective in the hands of those who already have legal expertise.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Allens closely supports the cluster’s principal proposition: LLMs can materially augment lawyers on bounded tasks, but performance remains uneven and current systems lack the contextual judgment and critical analysis required for reliable autonomous legal advice. Its benchmark evidence reinforces the cluster’s distinction between workflow gains and lawyer replacement, while supporting expert-led verification.
qs: That said, for a significant portion of tasks, LLMs can generate impressive responses that supplement and elevate lawyers’ work.
As our benchmarking shows, the current generation of large language models (LLMs) still falls short of the critical analysis skills required to deliver consistently reliable legal advice.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The Allens benchmark directly supports selective, human-led deployment: performance improved substantially but remained inconsistent across models, legal fields and questions; citation failures persisted; and current LLMs were useful mainly for bounded drafting, summarisation and high-level research under expert verification. Its design limitations also reinforce that benchmark performance does not establish general legal competence.
qs: These results illustrate that reasoning models do not necessarily outperform when executing legal analysis, and different models may perform better when answering different types of questions.

## We (still) need to talk about citations  The LLMs we tested produced a variety of incorrect, irrelevant and fictitious citations, which highlights the need for human verification of any citations produced.

kp.k: Expert benchmarking reports substantial annual performance improvements
kp.d: Allens assessed 7 publicly available LLM configurations against 30 Australian-law questions across 10 practice areas, using 23 senior legal experts in April 2025 and the standard of a lawyer with 5 years' post-admission experience. Each question was repeated three times, with scores allocated to substance (5), citations (3) and clarity (2). GPT-4o, OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 exceeded GPT-4's leading 2024 score; the report gives average substance scores of 4.3 out of 5 in 2025 versus 1.92 in 2024.
qs: Responses were evaluated on substance, citations and clarity by a panel of 23 senior Allens legal experts in April 2025.
GPT-4o, OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 each bettered 2024's highest score (achieved by GPT-4), particularly on

kp.k: High-quality answers remain limited and inconsistent
kp.d: Allens defines high quality as an average score of at least 8 out of 10 across three attempts at a question. OpenAI o1 and GPT-4o each scored above 8 on 6 of 30 questions; DeepSeek alone achieved 10 on all three attempts at any question. GPT-4o had a slightly higher average than o1, but o1 was more consistent. Most models occasionally gave mostly or completely incorrect answers, including fundamental legal errors, overseas-law substitutions and excessive confidence or agreement with the user.
qs: OpenAI o1 and GPT-4o produced the highest number of high-quality responses—each scoring above 8 in 6 out of the 30 benchmark questions—although DeepSeek was the only LLM to score a consistent perfect score of 10 out of 10 across all three attempts for any benchmark question.
the LLMs generally had a tendency to seek to confirm the user's input query rather than correct it, and several of the LLMs overstated the level of confidence in their advice.

kp.d: Every tested model sometimes supplied incorrect or fictional citations. Allens reports that underlying case law or legislation was absent or fabricated in 23% of answers; this is a combined absence-or-fabrication measure, not a standalone hallucination rate. Its detailed citation discussion says GPT-4o fabricated citations once and scored 1 out of 3 on 46% of responses, often because it relied on secondary sources or omitted legislative sections. The rubric assigns zero citation marks if even one citation is fictitious.
qs: The LLMs we tested produced a variety of incorrect, irrelevant and fictitious citations, which highlights the need for human verification of any citations produced.
Despite the request to provide citations, in 23% of answers the underlying case law or legislation was either completely absent or just made up.
The use of a single fictitious citation automatically leads to 0 marks being awarded.

kp.k: Reported citation averages differ between sections
kp.d: The report's category overview gives citation averages ranging from 1.19 for Gemini 1.5 to 1.60 for OpenAI o1, out of 3. Its later citation section instead gives Gemini 1.5 0.64, Gemini 2.0 1.21, and non-Gemini scores ranging from 1.16 for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, printed as 'Clause', to 1.62 for GPT-4o. That later section also says GPT-4o alone exceeded 50%. These are distinct figures reported within the source, rather than a single reconciled ranking.
qs: Gemini 1.5 was a clear outlier in citation performance, scoring only 0.64 out of 3 on average.
GPT-4o was the only model to score higher than 50% on citation (ie it was mostly correct, most of the time) and only provided fictitious citations in one instance.

kp.k: Jurisdictional contamination undermines Australian legal analysis
kp.d: Allens identifies intrusion of larger jurisdictions' legal principles as an ongoing risk for Australian practice. Nearly all responses to its patent question invoked the doctrine of equivalents, which the report says belongs to jurisdictions such as the US or UK but not Australia. Some responses fabricated Australian supporting cases; one GPT-4o response recognised the jurisdictional distinction but still claimed Canadian influence without citation.
qs: General purpose LLMs continue to struggle with the importance of jurisdiction.
Some other responses simply hallucinated fictitious Australian cases to support the application of the doctrine of equivalents.

kp.k: Reasoning models are not universally superior
kp.d: OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 performed well in difficult areas including tax, employment and dispute resolution. However, GPT-4o significantly outperformed o1 in banking and real estate, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 significantly outperformed other models in corporate law. Allens therefore treats model suitability as task-dependent and reports that improvements across newer models and generations were not linear.
qs: These results illustrate that reasoning models do not necessarily outperform when executing legal analysis, and different models may perform better when answering different types of questions.
Performance gains in newer models, and newer generations of the same model (eg between Gemini 1.5 and 2.0), were not linear.

kp.k: Web search creates performance and deployment trade-offs
kp.d: GPT-4o performed less effectively overall without web search, but search appeared to dilute some answers and did not necessarily improve citation quality. Allens observed that DeepSeek and Gemini 2.0 often supplied more citations than o1, but irrelevant or erroneous references reduced clarity. It speculates that o1's reasoning could contribute more to citation accuracy than live search and recommends weighing search access against security and business-specific fine-tuning when considering internal deployments.
qs: Overall, GPT-4o performed less effectively when its web search function was disabled. However, the advantage was not shown with every question. In some instances, web results appeared to have diluted the quality of the responses.
While DeepSeek and Gemini 2.0 frequently produced more citations than OpenAI o1, they were mostly irrelevant and erroneous, which diluted the clarity of otherwise accurate answers.

kp.k: Observed answer similarities suggest distillation to Allens
kp.d: Allens reports widely publicised claims about DeepSeek's distillation and low development and running costs rather than measuring those costs itself. It interprets similarities between DeepSeek and GPT-4o without web search as evidence of distillation, describing matching structure and substance across a significant number of questions. This is the report's interpretation of observed output similarities.
qs: DeepSeek's competitive performance is also notable in view of its widely reported low development and running cost.
For example, DeepSeek showed remarkable similarities to GPT-4o with web search disabled, in terms of both the structure and substance of its answers for a significant number of questions.

kp.k: Legal expertise remains central to safe AI use
kp.d: Allens favours lawyer augmentation rather than reliance on autonomous legal advice. It argues that current models lack the critical analysis, contextual sensitivity and expression of uncertainty needed for consistently reliable advice, and asserts that more data or training alone is unlikely to resolve these limitations. Its view that judgement, intuition, critical thinking and creativity remain uniquely human is a broader authorial claim, distinct from the benchmark scores. It recommends continued validation and verification by litigators, general counsel and other lawyers.
qs: As our benchmarking shows, the current generation of large language models (LLMs) still falls short of the critical analysis skills required to deliver consistently reliable legal advice.
These limitations are unlikely to be solved by simply adding more data or training—they stem from how LLMs work.
In legal practice, LLMs are safest and most effective in the hands of those who already have legal expertise.

kp.k: Drafting, summarisation and preliminary research offer practical applications
kp.d: Drawing on benchmarking and hands-on experience, Allens identifies initial correspondence and legal drafts, multimodal summarisation, and high-level research without specific citations as particularly effective applications, especially in well-understood, internationally harmonised areas. It predicts faster, more efficient advice with less research or specialist input, but warns that such advice may be incorrect. Continued performance improvement through citation safeguards and verification tools is an expectation rather than a tested outcome.
qs: AI-driven answer tools will likely allow legal advice to be delivered quickly and efficiently, with less need for 'time-consuming' research or specialist expertise. But that advice may not always be correct.
We expect their performance to continue improving, particularly as hallucinated citations are reduced through better safeguards and verification tools.
conducting high-level legal research in general practice areas without needing specific citations, especially in well-understood, internationally harmonised areas of law.

kp.k: Specialist products pursue vetted sources and workflow integration
kp.d: Allens describes legal-specific products trained on vetted legal materials, often US-focused, hybrid search linking answers to substantiating sources, multi-model functionality and assistants tailored to document summarisation and database searching. It suggests multi-model systems may eventually select the best model for each legal use case. Harvey, CoCounsel and Lexis+ AI were excluded from this benchmark because their specialised, structured or multi-model interactions are not directly comparable with general-purpose single-prompt testing.
qs: Developers have also begun tackling the citation problem by adopting 'hybrid search' techniques that combine LLM responses with links to substantiating vetted sources, in addition to beginning to integrate multi-model functionality into their solutions.

Our use of 'single prompt' questioning (for example) to ensure consistency between LLMs may not best demonstrate the capabilities of products that offer multiple structured pathways for answering the same question.

kp.k: Benchmark scope limits conclusions about professional substitution
kp.d: The repeated single-shot design measures relative model performance, not performance against a human control or the full range of legal workflows. Allens did not test iterative prompting, longer-document summarisation, contract extraction, stylistic revision or ideation, and only expects that richer prompting might improve results. Several newer releases were excluded because of time constraints. The source assumes lawyer use with review calibrated to average response quality and variability, and expressly disclaims reliance even on positively scored outputs.
qs: Unlike other studies, our benchmark does not include a human-lawyer "control" benchmark.
Such prompting, however, does not explore the results that can be achieved by carefully refining queries for each LLM or by interrogating and testing LLM responses in subsequent prompts.
No reliance should be placed on any LLMs or their responses, even in cases where specific answers or LLM performances have been positively marked.

kp.k: Published questions introduce possible benchmark contamination
kp.d: Using the same questions as 2024 supports longitudinal comparison, but Allens acknowledges that published commentary and sample answers may have entered model training or indexed responses. It says this could improve answers or reinforce prior responses. No word-for-word replication was detected, and the report calls for continued monitoring of over-fitting; contamination is therefore a stated possibility, not an established explanation for the measured gains.
qs: As the 2024 LinksAI and Allens AI Australian law benchmarks were published online, it is possible that commentary and sample responses from those reports may have been indexed and incorporated into the responses offered by any of the LLMs as part of the 2025 benchmark.

While we have not detected instances of word-for-word replication of 2024 responses, moderation for the over-fitting of LLM results to any responses that are publicly available will need to be monitored in coming years.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Allens claims that improving LLM performance creates opportunities for broad, lawyer-supervised use, but not consistently reliable autonomous legal advice.
pts.d: Allens reports substantial improvement over its 2024 benchmark, particularly in substance, while emphasising variable response quality and persistent incorrect or fabricated citations. It predicts faster, more efficient advice with less research and specialist input, but argues that current models lack the critical analysis, contextual sensitivity and expression of uncertainty needed for dependable advice. Its preferred model is augmentation: legally expert humans use and verify outputs. Allens also argues that the limitations arise from how LLMs work and are unlikely to be remedied simply through additional data or training; this is the firm's explanatory argument, rather than a separately tested benchmark result.

pts.k: Allens identifies drafting, summarisation and high-level research as useful applications, and anticipates further gains from safeguards and specialised legal products.
pts.d: Drawing on benchmarking and practical experience, Allens identifies initial correspondence and legal drafting, concise summaries of complex multimodal material, and general legal research that does not require specific citations as effective uses. It expects continuing improvement, particularly through citation safeguards and verification tools. It describes products grounded in vetted legal sources, hybrid search, multi-model functionality and workflow-specific legal assistants as developments that may improve task-specific results. These specialised products were not tested in the published benchmark, so the discussion is distinct from its comparative model findings.

pts.k: Allens argues that effective deployment requires task-specific model selection and human verification rather than assuming newer models, reasoning or web search always improve answers.
pts.d: Allens reports that reasoning models performed strongly on difficult specialist questions but were not uniformly superior: GPT-4o surpassed o1 in banking and real estate, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 excelled in corporate questions. Web access improved GPT-4o's overall performance but sometimes diluted individual answers. Allens identifies foreign-law intrusion, insufficient primary or pinpoint authority, fabricated citations, overconfidence and a tendency to affirm the user's premise as risks. It says businesses should balance web-search benefits against security and fine-tuning considerations, and lawyers should verify responses and citations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Allens' repeated, expert-graded Australian-law benchmark, supplemented by hands-on experience; broader forecasts are not direct productivity or replacement measurements.
pts.d: The firm reports testing seven LLM configurations, including GPT-4o with and without web search, on 30 questions across 10 practice areas, with three single-shot attempts per question. Twenty-three senior Allens experts evaluated responses in April 2025 against a five-years-post-admission Australian lawyer standard, allocating five marks for substance, three for citations and two for clarity. The same questions were used in 2024. Allens reports average substance scores rising from 1.92/5 to 4.3/5, and o1 and GPT-4o each exceeding 8/10 on six of 30 questions averaged across attempts. It reports absent or fabricated underlying authority in 23% of answers; that combined figure is not a fabrication-only rate. Citation averages and rankings differ between passages of the supplied report, so they do not supply one unambiguous numerical comparison. The benchmark has no human-lawyer control and does not measure delivered-service productivity, employment displacement or cost savings. Claims about practical drafting and summarisation also draw on hands-on experience; expectations about future improvements and hybrid products are prospective.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe the April 2025 assessment relative to 2024; future gains are undated and conditional on better reliability, verification and deployment choices.
pts.d: The published comparison concerns the tested publicly available chatbots, not all contemporary models or legal-AI products. Several newer releases were excluded because of time constraints, and Harvey, CoCounsel and Lexis+ AI were excluded to avoid inappropriate comparisons with specialised or multi-model systems. Single-shot prompting excludes iterative refinement and longer-form workflows; Allens expects more detailed prompts and follow-up interaction could improve results but leaves this to extension work. It acknowledges possible incorporation of published 2024 benchmark commentary and answers into later model responses, without detecting word-for-word replication. Broad adoption is conditional on managing reliability and citation risks, and review intensity depends on average output quality and variability. The report expressly disclaims reliance on tested outputs even when positively marked.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source principally concerns Australian practitioners, in-house counsel and deploying businesses, with particular risks for smaller jurisdictions.
pts.d: Australian lawyers across the ten tested practice areas may gain assistance with drafting, summaries and research while retaining responsibility for verification and professional judgement. Litigators and general counsel are explicitly addressed, covering both law-firm practice and the corporate buyer side. Businesses deploying internal tools face trade-offs involving search access, security and task-specific tuning. Australian users and those in other smaller jurisdictions face foreign-law contamination, while specialised legal datasets are described as often US-focused. Clients may receive advice faster and more efficiently, but the report makes no quantified claim about client savings, staffing reductions, firm leverage, pricing changes or access to justice.
